procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment(s) and order(s) passed by the High Court for the State of Telangana at Hyderabad in Criminal Petition Nos. 1146/2021 and 1147/ 2021, directing to enlarge respective respondent No. 1 on bail.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court allowed bail applications (Criminal Petition Nos. 1146/2021 and 1147/2021) and directed the release of Respondent No. 1 on bail in connection with offences under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Directorate of Enforcement appealed to the Supreme Court, feeling aggrieved and dissatisfied with the High Court's judgment(s) and order(s). The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, quashed the High Court's orders granting bail, and remitted the matters back to the High Court for fresh consideration of the bail applications, directing the accused to surrender within one week.

directions: The impugned judgment(s) and order(s) passed by the High Court in Criminal Petition Nos. 1146/2021 and 1147/2021 enlarging respective respondent No. 1 – accused in respective appeals on bail are hereby quashed and set aside.
Respective respondent No. 1 to surrender before the competent court having jurisdiction or before the concerned jail authority within a period of one week from today.

The matters are remitted back to the High Court to consider the bail applications afresh in light of the observations made hereinabove and after respective respondent No. 1 surrenders within a period of one week as ordered above.

issue.issue_text: Whether the filing of a chargesheet for the predicate offences can be a ground to grant bail for the scheduled offences under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, even if the investigation by the Enforcement Directorate is still ongoing.

facts: The accused were chargesheeted for predicate offenses under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Prevention of Corruption Act (PC Act).
Subsequently, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) initiated a separate investigation against them for scheduled offenses under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA).
The High Court granted bail to the accused, reasoning that the investigation was complete because a chargesheet had been filed for the predicate offenses.
The ED appealed this decision to the Supreme Court, arguing that its own investigation into the PMLA offenses was still ongoing.
law: Section 45 of the PMLA imposes stringent conditions for granting bail.

For a court to grant bail, it must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty of the offense and is not likely to commit any offense while on bail (the "twin conditions").

The investigation for predicate offenses (like those under the IPC or PC Act) is distinct and separate from the investigation for scheduled offenses conducted by the Enforcement Directorate under the PMLA.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's reasoning was flawed because it failed to distinguish between the two separate investigations.
The Court clarified that the investigation for the predicate offenses and the ED's investigation for the PMLA offenses are "different and distinct."
Therefore, the filing of a chargesheet for the predicate offenses was an "irrelevant consideration" for deciding bail in the PMLA case, especially since the ED's investigation was still in progress.

The Supreme Court also criticized the High Court for not considering the strict requirements ("rigour") of Section 45 of the PMLA and the seriousness of the money laundering allegations before granting bail.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's reasoning, holding that the filing of a chargesheet for predicate offenses cannot be a ground to grant bail for scheduled offenses under the PMLA while the Enforcement Directorate's investigation is still ongoing. The Court set aside the bail order and sent the matter back to the High Court for a fresh decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the acquittal or discharge of other co-accused in the predicate offences can be a valid ground for granting bail to an accused in a PMLA case.

facts: An accused was being investigated by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) for offences under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA).
The accused argued for bail, pointing out that other co-accused in the underlying 'predicate offences' (in this case, under the IPC and Prevention of Corruption Act) had been acquitted or discharged.
The High Court had granted bail to the accused.
The ED's investigation into the PMLA offences against this specific accused was still ongoing.
law: Section 45 of the PMLA imposes stringent conditions for granting bail in money laundering cases.
To grant bail under Section 45, a court must have reasonable grounds to believe that the accused is not guilty of the offence and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
The investigation for a predicate offence is considered separate and distinct from the investigation for a scheduled offence under the PMLA conducted by the ED.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had failed to consider the strict requirements ("rigour") of Section 45 of the PMLA when granting bail.

The Court explicitly stated that the acquittal or discharge of other co-accused in the predicate offence is not a valid ground to halt the PMLA investigation against the current accused or to grant them bail.

It reasoned that since the investigations for predicate and PMLA offences are distinct, developments in the former (like acquittals) do not automatically justify bail in the latter, especially while the ED's investigation is still active.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the acquittal or discharge of other co-accused in the predicate offences is not a valid ground for granting bail to an accused in a PMLA case. The court must independently assess the bail application against the strict conditions of Section 45 of the PMLA.

issue.issue_text: Whether the twin conditions for bail stipulated under Section 45 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 must be considered by the court while deciding a bail application under the Act.

facts: The accused was charged with predicate offenses under the Indian Penal Code and the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Subsequently, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) initiated a money laundering investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA).
The High Court granted bail to the accused.
The ED appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court had not properly applied the law.
law: Section 45 of the PMLA imposes stringent conditions for granting bail for an offense under the Act.

These "twin conditions" require that where the Public Prosecutor opposes the bail application, the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is (1) not guilty of the offense and (2) not likely to commit any offense while on bail.
These conditions are in addition to the general limitations on granting bail under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had erred by failing to consider the "rigour of Section 45 of the PML Act, 2002" when it granted bail.
The Court clarified that the investigation for the predicate offenses is distinct from the investigation for money laundering under the PMLA.

Therefore, the fact that a chargesheet may have been filed for the predicate offenses is not a valid reason to grant bail for the PMLA offense without considering Section 45, especially while the ED's investigation is still ongoing.
The Supreme Court also noted that the High Court failed to consider the seriousness of the money laundering allegations.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's order granting bail was unsustainable because it did not consider the mandatory twin conditions stipulated in Section 45 of the PMLA. The Court set aside the bail order and sent the case back to the High Court for a fresh decision, explicitly directing it to consider the requirements of Section 45.

appellant_arguments: The High Court has not properly appreciated and/or considered the seriousness of the offences which are scheduled offences under the PML Act, 2002.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When considering a bail application for an offence under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, a court must consider the stringent conditions and limitations stipulated in Section 45 of that Act.
obiter: The acquittal or discharge of other co-accused in the predicate offence is not, by itself, a ground to discontinue an investigation against another accused for the same offence.
An ongoing enquiry or investigation into scheduled offences is sufficient at the bail stage, even if the accused was not initially named in the FIR for the predicate offence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's orders granting bail are unsustainable because it failed to consider the mandatory rigour of Section 45 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. The High Court also did not consider the seriousness of the alleged scheduled offences and overlooked the crucial fact that the investigation by the Enforcement Directorate was still ongoing, making the grant of bail improper.
legal_tests_applied: The twin conditions for bail under Section 45 of the PML Act, 2002 must be satisfied: "(i) the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application for such release; and (ii) where the Public Prosecutor opposes the application, the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail:"
why_respondent_won: The High Court erred by granting bail without considering the mandatory twin conditions stipulated under Section 45 of the PML Act, 2002.

The acquittal or discharge of other co-accused in the predicate offences is not a valid ground for granting bail in the PMLA case, as the court found that "merely because other accused are acquitted/ discharged, it cannot be a ground not to continue the investigation in respect of respective respondent No. 1."

The filing of a chargesheet in the predicate offences is not a sufficient ground for bail because the High Court "has not at all considered the fact that the investigation by the Enforcement Directorate for the scheduled offences under the PML Act, 2002 is still going on."
policy_considerations: The court must consider the "seriousness of the offences which are scheduled offences under the PML Act, 2002" when deciding on a bail application, reflecting the legislative intent to treat such economic offences with greater stringency.
